name: Dex Horthy
role: Founder/CEO of HumanLayer; author of 12-factor-agents and 'advanced context engineering' (research-plan-implement)

sources.title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases (ace-fca.md)
No Vibes Allowed: Solving Hard Problems in Complex Codebases (AI Engineer talk)
Writing a good CLAUDE.md (HumanLayer blog, author Kyle)

philosophy: Today's models can work in large codebases if the whole workflow is built around managing context. Keep context use around 40-60%, compact often into written artifacts, and put human review on the research and the plan, where it has the most leverage.
process: Research: parallel read-only subagents (locator/analyzer/pattern-finder) map how the system works and write a research doc to thoughts/
Human reviews the research and discards or redoes it if wrong
Plan: write a phased implementation plan with files, snippets and success criteria; iterate with the human
Implement phase by phase and run verification after each phase

For complex work, compact the current status back into the plan file after each verified phase (the HumanLayer team repo also had create_handoff/resume_handoff commands, mostly written by Kyle Mistele; Dex does not describe them in his write-up)
Optional extras from the HumanLayer team repo: validate_plan checks the work against the plan and describe_pr drafts the PR (not part of Dex's published research/plan/implement write-up)

Newer flow in HumanLayer's company plugin (rpi v0.50.0, author 'HumanLayer'): research questions, research, design discussion, structure outline, plan, implement, iterate. This is a company product; Dex's own description of it (talk 'From RPI to QRSPI') was not checked

name: Armin Ronacher
role: Creator of Flask/Jinja; co-founder of Earendil; prolific writer on agentic coding

sources.title: Agentic Coding Things That Didn't Work
Pi: The Minimal Agent Within OpenClaw

philosophy: Simple, fast, observable tooling (Makefile, log files, CLIs) beats clever automation. Talk to the agent a lot, often by voice, and keep only automations you actually use. He prefers skills that wrap CLIs over MCP.
process: Make the dev environment agent-friendly: Makefile targets, a process manager that refuses double starts, all output logged to files
Keep audio input going and dump your full train of thought into the prompt, then let the agent work while rarely interrupting
Run with permissions skipped, isolated (Docker / separate checkouts) for parallel work
Use subagents only for investigative/read-only tasks
Steer tool use with PATH interceptors (e.g. force uv) instead of hooks
Plan through a back-and-forth of questions instead of plan mode ('I don't use plan mode'); his agent-stuff package includes a /discuss interviewer prompt for Pi
Delete automations/skills that stop being used

name: Mitchell Hashimoto
role: Co-founder of HashiCorp; creator of Ghostty terminal
philosophy: Use real agents, not chat. Get good at them by redoing your own work, and when an agent makes a mistake, fix the harness (AGENTS.md, scripts) so it does not happen again. Never ship AI code you don't understand or haven't reviewed.
process: Split work into clear tasks; separate planning sessions from execution sessions
Plan with a slow read-only 'oracle' model and save the plan as a spec file
Give agents ways to verify themselves (filtered test scripts, screenshot scripts)
Use the last 30 minutes of the day for background agents (research, exploration, issue triage that only writes reports)
Each morning hand off sure-win tasks to a single background agent; turn agent notifications off
When an agent repeats a mistake, update AGENTS.md (per-directory) or add a tool
Review everything manually before merging; rewrite parts by hand when needed

skills.description: Ghostty project skill for writing git commit messages

settings.notes: Turn off agent desktop notifications. Keep per-directory AGENTS.md files (Ghostty has 10). Ghostty's AI policy requires outside contributors to disclose AI use; maintainers are explicitly exempt, so this is a project rule, not Mitchell's personal setting.

unverified: Authorship of the Ghostty skill by Mitchell personally

The writing-commit-messages skill has two commit authors, Jon Parise and Mitchell Hashimoto. It is Ghostty team work, not Mitchell's alone.
'zig build' and 'nushell scripts' come from the Ghostty project (AGENTS.md; .agents/commands/review-branch, written by Mitchell), not from a statement of his personal tools.
The adoption post names GPT-5.2-Codex through Amp deep mode. It also says he does not run multiple agents at once.

Iterate with screenshots and short prompts; queue 'continue' messages for long tasks
Have the model write tests in the same context after each feature
Agents commit only their own files ('commit/push'); land PRs with /landpr-style prompts
Keep a global AGENTS.md updated whenever something goes wrong

name: Harper Reed
role: CEO of 2389 Research; former CTO of Obama 2012 campaign
philosophy: Spec, then plan, then execute in small steps. Hone the idea one question at a time, turn it into small TDD prompts, and let the agent work through them. Tests, linters and pre-commit hooks keep it honest.
process: Idea honing: a chat LLM asks one question at a time, giving spec.md
Planning: a reasoning model turns the spec into small TDD steps (prompt_plan.md) plus todo.md
Execution: Claude Code takes the next unmarked prompt, implements it with tests, verifies, commits, and marks it done
After each prompt Claude pauses for your review or feedback; plans are usually 8-12 steps
Pre-commit hooks run tests/types/lint on every commit; formatters (ruff, biome, clippy)
Fresh-eyes review of new code via a subagent (careful-review)
Existing codebases: repomix + llm CLI via mise tasks for reviews/issues/missing tests

sources.title: Introducing Beads: A Coding Agent Memory System

philosophy: Agents forget between sessions, and markdown TODO plans rot. Give them a dependency-aware issue graph they query for ready work and update as they go, and scale by orchestrating many agents (Gas Town).
process: Install bd once and run bd init per repo (writes AGENTS.md section and agent hooks)
bd prime is injected at SessionStart/PreCompact to restore workflow context
Agent runs bd ready to pick unblocked work and claims it (bd update <id> --claim)
File newly discovered work as issues with dependencies (bd create, bd dep add) instead of markdown TODOs
Close issues and store durable facts (bd close, bd remember) before ending the session
Scale to many parallel agents with Gas Town (gt)

name: Thorsten Ball
role: Co-creator of Amp (coding agent), previously at Sourcegraph and Zed; author of 'Writing an Interpreter in Go' and 'How to Build an Agent'

sources.title: Think Harder: How I Prompt (Laracon US talk)

philosophy: An agent is 'an LLM, a loop, and enough tokens' (an LLM with access to tools). Treat each prompt as a briefing: how is the model supposed to know what I mean? Move the 'how to do things' into the codebase (AGENTS.md files). He currently uses no MCP servers or custom slash commands.
process: You make the architecture decisions; the prompt spells out files, commits and constraints ('paint by numbers')
Two-step prompt: first have the agent find/load context, then make the request
Attach screenshots generously; give the agent visual feedback (Playwright/Storybook)
Start new threads often (quality drops beyond ~100k tokens)
Stage good changes in git, discard the rest; ask the agent to review its own diff
Put AGENTS.md files throughout the codebase; review load-bearing code closely

settings.notes: As of the Laracon US talk (2026-07-29) he uses no MCP servers, no custom slash commands, and only one or two skills, and builds custom tools as Amp plugins. He gives the agent a 'super long leash' and documents wherever it fails. In 2025 he used the Playwright and postgres MCP servers (How I Use Amp, now archived).
